ambidextrous

am-bih-DEK-struhs · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Ambidextrous is able to use both the right and left hand equally well.

Growing up ambidextrous, she never had to decide which hand to favor when learning to play tennis.

Example

The famous painter trained himself to be ambidextrous later in life, switching brushes between hands whenever one arm grew tired.

He wasn't born naturally able to use both hands -- he deliberately built the skill, but the end result, equal comfort with either hand, is still what ambidextrous means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

two-handed: A two-handed grip, swing, or catch uses both hands together at once on the same task. Ambidextrous makes a different claim: each hand alone is equally capable, so the person can switch freely between them. A tennis player's two-handed backhand proves nothing about whether she is ambidextrous.

dexterous: Dexterous means skillful with the hands -- quick, precise, sure-fingered. A dexterous person may still do everything with one favored hand. Ambidextrous adds the rarer claim that the right and left hands are equally good, so neither one is ever the wrong hand for the job.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

one-sided: favoring or able to use only one hand or side

clumsy: lacking skill or grace, especially with the hands

Where it sits · how impressive the physical skill is — handy → ambidextrous → virtuosic

handy vs. ambidextrous: Handy is a weaker level of skill than ambidextrous: a handy person is reasonably good with their hands, while an ambidextrous one goes further, using both hands equally well.

virtuosic vs. ambidextrous: Virtuosic goes further than ambidextrous: being ambidextrous means using both hands equally well, but virtuosic skill is more extreme, an extraordinary, dazzling mastery of a craft or art.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ambi-

Prefix — ambi-: both (Latin)

Root — dextr-

Root — dextr-: right hand (and, by extension, skill) (from Latin dexter, 'right-hand, skillful' -- the source of dexterity)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Ambidextrous comes from Latin ambi- ('both') + dextr- (from dexter, 'right hand' -- also the source of skill-words like dexterity) + -ous ('full of') -- literally 'full of right-handedness on both sides,' or equally skilled with either hand.

Use the root in a new word: dexterity

Ambidextrous describes genuine, trained equal skill with both hands -- don't use it loosely for someone who is just generally good at many things.
